more.title: More of the German Sentence
more.desc: One word is missing from a German sentence: a verb in another person, a personal pronoun in its case, a noun or article in the dative or the genitive, a word joined by und, or a word of place. The word is chosen from tiles at the first levels and written at the higher ones.

intro.h: Persons. German writes the subject pronoun, and the verb agrees with it in person and number.
eg: wir lesen das Buch; du liest das Buch

intro.h: The pronoun. The personal pronoun has four cases, as the article does.
eg: der König sieht mich; der König gibt mir das Buch; ich danke dir

intro.h: The dative and the genitive. The one who receives is in the dative, and the possessor in the genitive. The dative plural of a noun adds -n.
eg: der Mann gibt dem König das Buch; den Freunden; das Pferd des Königs

intro.h: Und. Two subjects joined by und take a plural verb, and two nouns joined by und share the case of their use.
eg: der König und die Frau lesen das Buch; ich helfe dem Mann und der Frau

intro.h: Place. In takes the dative for the place where and the accusative for the place to which; aus takes the dative; nach stands before a city or a country.
eg: in der Stadt, in die Stadt; im Haus, ins Haus; aus dem Haus; nach Berlin

items.en: We read the book.
items.why: Wir is the first person plural, and its verb ends in -en: wir lesen. Liest is the second or third person singular, lest the second person plural, and lese the first person singular.

items.en: You (one friend) read the book.
items.why: Du is the second person singular, and lesen changes e to ie in that person and the next: du liest, er liest. Lest is the second person plural.

items.en: He speaks with the king.
items.why: Er is the third person singular, and sprechen changes e to i in the second and third persons singular: er spricht. Sprecht is the second person plural.

items.en: I give the woman the book.
items.why: Ich is the first person singular, and its verb ends in -e without a change of vowel: ich gebe. Gibst and gibt are the second and third persons singular.

items.en: You (several friends) are in the garden.
items.why: Ihr is the second person plural, and the form of sein for that person is seid. Sind is the first or third person plural.

items.en: The king has a horse.
items.why: Der König is a third person singular subject, and the form of haben for that person is hat. Hast is the second person singular, and habt the second person plural.

items.en: They come from the city.
items.why: Sie here is the third person plural, they, and its verb ends in -en: sie kommen. Kommt is the third person singular or the second person plural.

items.en: The friend sees the sea.
items.why: Der Freund is a third person singular subject, and sehen changes e to ie in that person: er sieht. Siehst is the second person singular.

items.en: The king sees me.
items.why: Sehen takes a direct object in the accusative, and the accusative of ich is mich. Mir is the dative, and mein the possessive.

items.en: The king gives me the book.
items.why: The one who receives is in the dative, and the dative of ich is mir. Mich is the accusative.

items.en: The woman sees him.
items.why: The direct object is in the accusative, and the accusative of er is ihn. Ihm is the dative.

items.en: The woman gives him the book.
items.why: The one who receives is in the dative, and the dative of er is ihm. Ihn is the accusative.

items.en: The king helps her.
items.why: Helfen takes the dative, and the dative of sie, she, is ihr. Sie would be the accusative, and ihnen is plural.

items.en: I thank you (one friend).
items.why: Danken takes the dative, and the dative of du is dir. Dich is the accusative.

items.en: The book is for us.
items.why: Für takes the accusative, and the accusative of wir is uns. Unser is the genitive, and euch belongs to ihr.

items.en: We speak with them.
items.why: Mit takes the dative, and the dative of sie, they, is ihnen. Sie is the accusative.

items.en: The man gives the king the book.
items.fr: Der Mann gibt ______ König das Buch.
items.why: The king receives the book, so he is in the dative, and the dative of der is dem. Den is the accusative, and des the genitive.

items.en: The man gives the woman the book.
items.fr: Der Mann gibt ______ Frau das Buch.
items.why: Frau is feminine, and the feminine dative of the article is der. Die is the nominative or accusative.

items.en: The king gives the friends a horse.
items.fr: Der König gibt den ______ ein Pferd.
items.why: The dative plural of a noun adds -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s: den Freunden.

items.en: The king answers the woman.
items.why: Antworten takes the dative of the person answered, and the feminine dative is der.

items.en: She sends the man a book.
items.why: The dative singular of Mann has no ending today: dem Mann. Mannes is the genitive, and Männern the dative plural.

items.en: We show the friend the garden.
items.why: The friend is the one shown, in the dative, so dem Freund. Den Garten, the thing shown, is the accusative.

items.en: The woman gives the men the books.
items.fr: Die Frau gibt ______ Männern die Bücher.
items.why: The dative plural of the article is den for every gender, and the noun adds -n: den Männern.

items.en: The king helps the friend.
items.why: Helfen takes the dative, so dem Freund. Den would be the accusative.

items.en: The king’s horse is large.
items.why: The possessor is in the genitive, and the masculine genitive of the article is des, with -s on the noun: des Königs.

items.en: The woman’s house is small.
items.why: The feminine genitive of the article is der, and a feminine noun adds no ending: der Frau.

items.en: The man’s book is good.
items.why: A strong masculine noun adds -es or -s in the genitive singular: des Mannes.

items.en: The garden of the house is large.
items.why: Haus is neuter, and a strong neuter noun adds -es in the genitive singular: des Hauses.

items.en: The friends’ house is old.
items.why: The genitive plural of the article is der for every gender: der Freunde.

items.en: Because of the king she stays.
items.why: Wegen takes the genitive in written German, so des Königs.

items.en: During the day he works.
items.why: Während takes the genitive, and Tag is masculine: des Tages.

items.en: The man’s son is here.
items.why: The possessor is in the genitive, and the masculine genitive of the article is des.

items.en: The king and the woman read the book.
items.fr: Der König und die Frau ______ das Buch.
items.why: Two subjects joined by und make a plural subject of the third person, so lesen.

items.en: The man and the woman are good.
items.fr: Der Mann und die Frau sind ______.
items.why: An adjective that is the predicate, after sein, takes no ending: sie sind gut.

items.en: I see the king and the woman.
items.fr: Ich sehe den König und ______ Frau.
items.why: Both nouns are the object of sehe, so both are in the accusative, and the feminine accusative is die.

items.en: I help the man and the woman.
items.fr: Ich helfe dem Mann und ______ Frau.
items.why: Helfen takes the dative, and both nouns joined by und are in that case, so der Frau.

items.en: You and I, we are friends.
items.why: A subject that includes the speaker is of the first person plural, so wir sind.

items.en: My friend and I go into the city.
items.fr: Mein Freund und ich ______ in die Stadt.
items.why: Mein Freund und ich includes the speaker, so the verb is in the first person plural: gehen.

items.en: The book and the house belong to the king.
items.fr: Das Buch und das Haus ______ dem König.
items.why: Two subjects joined by und take a plural verb: sie gehören.

items.en: He gives the man and the friend a horse.
items.fr: Er gibt dem Mann und ______ Freund ein Pferd.
items.why: Both receive the horse, so both are in the dative: dem Mann und dem Freund.

items.en: The king is in the city.
items.why: In takes the dative for the place where, and the feminine dative is der.

items.en: The king goes into the city.
items.why: In takes the accusative for the place to which, and the feminine accusative is die.

items.en: The book is in the house.
items.why: The place where takes in with the dative, and in dem contracts to im.

items.en: He goes into the house.
items.why: The place to which takes in with the accusative, and in das contracts to ins.

items.en: The woman comes out of the house.
items.why: Aus always takes the dative, so aus dem Haus.

items.en: He travels to Berlin.
items.why: Before the name of a city or a country without an article, motion toward is shown by nach.

items.en: She goes to the friend.
items.why: Motion toward a person is shown by zu with the dative, and zu dem contracts to zum. Zur is zu der, for a feminine noun.

items.en: The horse stands in the garden.
items.why: Im is in with the dative, and the dative singular of Garten has no ending. Gärten is the plural, and Gartens the genitive.

voice.title: The Passive, the Infinitive, and the Participle in German
voice.desc: One word is missing from a German sentence: the passive auxiliary or participle, the doer with von, a reflexive pronoun, an infinitive with or without zu, or a participle with its ending.

intro.h: The passive. The passive is werden with the past participle, and the doer is introduced by von. In the Perfekt of the passive the participle of werden is worden.
eg: das Buch wird von dem König gelesen; das Haus ist verkauft worden

intro.h: The infinitive. A modal verb takes the infinitive without zu; most other verbs take zu; and um ... zu gives a purpose.
eg: ich will lesen; sie versucht, das Buch zu verstehen; um ein Haus zu kaufen

intro.h: The participle. The past participle stands at the end of the clause in the Perfekt, and a participle before a noun takes the adjective endings.
eg: der König hat gesprochen; das gelesene Buch; mit dem gekauften Pferd

items.en: The book is read by the king.
items.fr: Das Buch wird von dem König ______.
items.why: The passive is werden with the past participle, and the participle stands at the end of the clause: wird gelesen.

items.en: The books are read.
items.why: The passive auxiliary agrees with the subject, die Bücher, which is plural: werden.

items.en: The horse is sold by the man.
items.fr: Das Pferd wird ______ dem Mann verkauft.
items.why: The doer in a German passive is introduced by von with the dative.

items.en: The letter was written by the woman.
items.fr: Der Brief ______ von der Frau geschrieben.
items.why: The past passive uses the Präteritum of werden, wurde. Wird is the present, and würde the Konjunktiv II.

items.en: The house has been sold.
items.why: In the Perfekt of the passive the participle of werden is worden, not geworden.

items.en: He is being helped.
items.why: Helfen takes the dative, so the passive has no subject in the nominative, and the verb stands in the third person singular: ihm wird geholfen.

items.en: The man washes himself.
items.why: The reflexive pronoun of the third person is sich. Ihn would be another man.

items.en: The book reads easily.
items.why: A reflexive verb can have a sense close to the passive: das Buch liest sich leicht.

items.en: I want to read the book.
items.why: A modal verb such as wollen takes the infinitive without zu, at the end of the clause.

items.en: He can come tomorrow.
items.why: Können takes the infinitive without zu: er kann kommen.

items.en: She tries to understand the book.
items.why: After versuchen the infinitive takes zu, and it stands at the end of its clause: zu verstehen.

items.en: He works in order to buy a house.
items.fr: Er arbeitet, ______ ein Haus zu kaufen.
items.why: Purpose with the same subject is given by um with zu and the infinitive: um ein Haus zu kaufen.

items.en: It is easy to read the book.
items.fr: Es ist leicht, das Buch ______ lesen.
items.why: After an adjective such as leicht the infinitive takes zu: das Buch zu lesen.

items.en: I hear the king sing.
items.why: Hören and sehen take the infinitive without zu: ich höre den König singen.

items.en: We must go home.
items.why: Müssen is a modal verb and takes the infinitive without zu.

items.en: He begins to write.
items.why: Beginnen takes the infinitive with zu: er beginnt zu schreiben.

items.en: The king has spoken.
items.why: The Perfekt is haben with the past participle, and the participle of the strong verb sprechen is gesprochen.

items.en: The woman has come.
items.why: Kommen forms the Perfekt with sein, and its participle is gekommen.

items.en: We have made the bed.
items.why: Machen is a weak verb, and its participle is ge- with the stem and -t: gemacht.

items.en: the book that has been read
items.why: A participle used as an adjective before its noun takes the adjective endings, and after das the ending is -e: das gelesene Buch.

items.en: with the bought horse
items.why: Mit takes the dative, and after dem the adjective ending is -en: mit dem gekauften Pferd.

items.en: the singing woman
items.why: The present participle used as an adjective takes the adjective endings, and after die in the nominative singular the ending is -e.

items.en: He has gone into the city.
items.why: Gehen forms the Perfekt with sein, and its participle is gegangen.

items.en: The man has arrived.
items.why: In the participle of a verb with a separable prefix, ge- stands between the prefix and the stem: angekommen.

clause.title: Clauses and the Order of Words in German
clause.desc: One word is missing from a German sentence: a relative pronoun in its case, a word in a clause of cause, a word in a condition with wenn, a word in a reported statement or question, or a word in an infinitive or participial phrase.

intro.h: The relative. The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from its noun and its case from its own clause, and the verb of the relative clause goes to the end.
eg: der Mann, der spricht; der Mann, den ich sehe; der Mann, dem ich helfe; die Frau, deren Haus groß ist

intro.h: Cause. After weil and da the finite verb goes to the end; after denn it stays in the second place.
eg: weil er krank ist; denn er ist müde

intro.h: Condition. A real condition takes the indicative; a condition that is not real takes the Konjunktiv II, and its result is usually würde with the infinitive.
eg: wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause; wenn ich Zeit hätte, würde ich kommen

intro.h: Reported speech. A reported statement can begin with dass, a reported yes-or-no question with ob; written German often reports speech in the Konjunktiv I.
eg: er sagt, dass der König krank ist; ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt; er sagt, er sei krank

intro.h: Phrases. Um, ohne, and statt take zu with the infinitive, and a participle with its own phrase can stand before a noun.
eg: ohne ein Wort zu sagen; das auf dem Tisch liegende Buch

items.en: The man who speaks is my friend.
items.fr: Der Mann, ______ spricht, ist mein Freund.
items.why: The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from der Mann and its case from its own clause, where it is the subject: der.

items.en: The man whom I see is the king.
items.fr: Der Mann, ______ ich sehe, ist der König.
items.why: The relative is the object of sehe, so it is in the accusative: den.

items.en: The man whom I help is my friend.
items.fr: Der Mann, ______ ich helfe, ist mein Freund.
items.why: Helfen takes the dative, so the relative is dem.

items.en: The woman whose house is large is here.
items.fr: Die Frau, ______ Haus groß ist, ist hier.
items.why: The relative that shows the possessor is in the genitive, and for a feminine antecedent it is deren.

items.en: The man whose horse is old is here.
items.fr: Der Mann, ______ Pferd alt ist, ist hier.
items.why: For a masculine antecedent, the genitive relative is dessen.

items.en: The book that I read is long.
items.fr: Das Buch, ______ ich lese, ist lang.
items.why: The relative of a neuter noun in the accusative is das, with one s. Dass is the conjunction that.

items.en: The women who come are friends.
items.why: The relative of a plural noun in the nominative is die.

items.en: The men with whom I speak are here.
items.fr: Die Männer, mit ______ ich spreche, sind hier.
items.why: Mit takes the dative, and the dative plural of the relative is denen.

items.en: He stays at home because he is ill.
items.fr: Er bleibt zu Hause, weil er krank ______.
items.why: After weil the finite verb goes to the end of the clause, and the clause states a fact, so the indicative: weil er krank ist.

items.en: She reads because she has time.
items.why: After weil the verb stands last, in the indicative: weil sie Zeit hat.

items.en: We stay because it is raining.
items.why: After weil the verb stands last: weil es regnet.

items.en: He stays because he is tired.
items.why: The verb stands at the end, so the clause is subordinate, and weil gives the reason. Denn would keep the order of a main clause: denn er ist müde.

items.en: He stays, for he is tired.
items.why: The verb stands second, as in a main clause, so the joining word is the coordinating denn. After weil the verb would go to the end.

items.en: I know that he is coming tomorrow.
items.why: After dass the finite verb goes to the end: dass er morgen kommt.

items.en: Since the king is ill, the queen speaks.
items.fr: Da der König krank ist, ______ die Königin.
items.why: When a subordinate clause stands first, it fills the first place, and the verb of the main clause follows it at once: spricht die Königin.

items.en: If I had time, I would come.
items.fr: Wenn ich Zeit ______, würde ich kommen.
items.why: A condition that is not real takes the Konjunktiv II: wenn ich Zeit hätte. Hatte is the Präteritum.

items.en: If I had time, I would come.
items.fr: Wenn ich Zeit hätte, ______ ich kommen.
items.why: The result of a condition that is not real is given by würde with the infinitive. Wurde is the Präteritum.

items.en: If he were king, he would be happy.
items.fr: Wenn er König ______, wäre er glücklich.
items.why: A condition that is not real takes the Konjunktiv II: wenn er König wäre. War is the Präteritum.

items.en: If it rains, we stay at home.
items.fr: Wenn es ______, bleiben wir zu Hause.
items.why: A real condition takes the indicative, and after wenn the verb goes to the end: wenn es regnet.

items.en: If you come, I am glad.
items.why: Du takes the ending -st, and after wenn the verb goes to the end: wenn du kommst.

items.en: If you come, I am glad.
items.why: The main clause follows the subordinate clause, so its verb stands first, and ich takes -e: freue ich mich.

items.en: If we had the book, we would read it.
items.fr: Wenn wir das Buch hätten, ______ wir es lesen.
items.why: The result is würde with the infinitive, in the first person plural: würden wir es lesen.

items.en: He says that the king is ill.
items.fr: Er sagt, ______ der König krank ist.
items.why: A reported statement can be introduced by dass, with two s, and its verb goes to the end. Das is the article or the relative.

items.en: I do not know whether he is coming.
items.why: A reported yes-or-no question is introduced by ob.

items.en: He asks where the king is.
items.why: A reported question keeps its question word, and its verb goes to the end: wo der König ist.

items.en: She asks what he wants.
items.why: The question is about the thing wanted, so was. Wer asks about a person.

items.en: I believe that she is right.
items.why: After dass the verb goes to the end, and sie, she, takes hat.

items.en: He says that he is ill.
items.why: Written German reports speech in the Konjunktiv I, and the third person singular of sein is sei. Without dass the reported clause keeps the order of a main clause.

items.en: She says that she has no time.
items.why: The Konjunktiv I of haben in the third person singular is habe, the form of reported speech.

items.en: He says that he is coming tomorrow.
items.why: The Konjunktiv I of kommen in the third person singular is komme.

items.en: He left without saying a word.
items.fr: Er ging, ______ ein Wort zu sagen.
items.why: Ohne with zu and the infinitive says that something did not happen: ohne ein Wort zu sagen.

items.en: Instead of working, he sleeps.
items.why: Statt with zu and the infinitive gives what is done in place of something else.

items.en: He came in order to see the king.
items.fr: Er kam, um den König zu ______.
items.why: Um ... zu takes the infinitive at the end: um den König zu sehen.

items.en: He speaks loudly so that the king hears him.
items.fr: Er spricht laut, ______ der König ihn hört.
items.why: When the subject of the purpose clause is not the subject of the main clause, German uses damit with a finite verb. Um ... zu needs the same subject.

items.en: the book lying on the table
items.why: A participle with its own phrase can stand before the noun, and it takes the adjective ending: das auf dem Tisch liegende Buch.

items.en: the man who has arrived in the city
items.why: The participle stands before the noun with its phrase and takes the ending -e after der: der in der Stadt angekommene Mann.

mood.title: The Konjunktiv and the Imperative
mood.desc: One word is missing from a German sentence, or one form of a verb is asked for: the Konjunktiv II and its uses, the Konjunktiv I of reported speech, or the imperative.

intro.h: The Konjunktiv II. The Konjunktiv II of a strong verb is made from the Präteritum, with the umlaut and -e; with other verbs German usually uses würde with the infinitive.
eg: wäre, hätte, würde, käme; ich würde bleiben

intro.h: Its uses. The Konjunktiv II gives what is imagined or not real: a condition, its result, a wish, or a polite request.
eg: wenn ich nur Zeit hätte!; das wäre gut; würden Sie das Fenster öffnen?

intro.h: The Konjunktiv I. The Konjunktiv I is made from the stem of the infinitive with -e, and its chief use is reported speech in written German.
eg: er sei, er habe, er komme; er sagt, er sei krank

intro.h: The imperative. The imperative singular has no ending or -e, and verbs that change e to i or ie in the present change it here too. The plural is the ihr form, and the formal imperative keeps Sie.
eg: komm!, lies!, gib!; kommt!; sprechen Sie!

items.en: Konjunktiv II, first person singular, of “sein.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of sein is made from the Präteritum war with the umlaut and -e: ich wäre.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of “haben.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of haben is hätte, from hatte with the umlaut.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of “werden.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of werden is würde, from wurde with the umlaut.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, first person singular, of “können.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of können is könnte. Konnte is the Präteritum, and könne the Konjunktiv I.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of “kommen.”
items.why: A strong verb makes its Konjunktiv II from the Präteritum, with the umlaut and -e: kam, käme.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, first person plural, of “sein.”
items.why: The first person plural of the Konjunktiv II of sein is wären. Waren is the Präteritum.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, third person singular, of “müssen.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of müssen is müsste. Musste is the Präteritum.

items.en: Konjunktiv II, first person singular, of “wissen.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv II of wissen is wüsste. Wusste is the Präteritum.

items.en: If only I had time!
items.why: A wish that is not fulfilled takes the Konjunktiv II: wenn ich nur Zeit hätte!

items.en: Would you open the window?
items.why: Würde with the infinitive makes a polite request: würden Sie das Fenster öffnen?

items.en: In your place I would stay.
items.why: Würde with the infinitive says what would happen: ich würde bleiben.

items.en: He acts as if he were the king.
items.fr: Er tut so, als ______ er der König.
items.why: After als in the sense of as if, the verb follows at once and stands in the Konjunktiv II: als wäre er der König.

items.en: If I were rich, I would buy a house.
items.fr: Wenn ich reich wäre, ______ ich ein Haus kaufen.
items.why: The result of a condition that is not real is würde with the infinitive.

items.en: I wish that he would come.
items.why: A wish takes the Konjunktiv II, and the Konjunktiv II of kommen is käme.

items.en: That would be good.
items.why: What would be so is said with the Konjunktiv II: das wäre gut.

items.en: I would have read the book if I had had time.
items.fr: Ich ______ das Buch gelesen, wenn ich Zeit gehabt hätte.
items.why: A past condition that was not fulfilled takes the Konjunktiv II of the auxiliary with the participle: ich hätte gelesen. Lesen forms its Perfekt with haben.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “sein.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I of sein in the third person singular is sei, the form of reported speech.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “haben.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I is made from the stem of the infinitive with -e: er habe.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “kommen.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I takes the stem of the infinitive and -e: er komme.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “werden.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I of werden is er werde. Wird is the indicative, and würde the Konjunktiv II.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “können.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I is made from the stem of the infinitive, so it keeps the umlaut of können: er könne.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person plural, of “sein.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I of sein in the third person plural is seien.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “sprechen.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I keeps the vowel of the infinitive, without the change to i: er spreche.

items.en: Konjunktiv I, third person singular, of “geben.”
items.why: The Konjunktiv I keeps the vowel of the infinitive: er gebe. Gibt is the indicative, and gäbe the Konjunktiv II.

items.en: (To one friend) Read the book!
items.why: A strong verb that changes e to ie in the present also changes it in the imperative singular, and the imperative has no -st: lies!

items.en: (To one friend) Give me the book!
items.why: The imperative singular of geben is gib, with the change of e to i.

items.en: (To several friends) Come here!
items.why: The imperative addressed to several friends is the ihr form without the pronoun: kommt!

items.en: (Formal) Speak slowly, please!
items.why: The formal imperative keeps the pronoun Sie after the verb: sprechen Sie!

items.en: (To one friend) Speak louder!
items.why: The imperative singular of sprechen is sprich, with the change of e to i.

items.en: (To one friend) Be quiet!
items.why: The imperative singular of sein is sei. Seid is the plural.

items.en: (To one friend) Come here!
items.why: The imperative singular of kommen is komm, and the ending -e is usually left off.

items.en: Let us go!
items.why: An imperative that includes the speaker puts the verb first with wir: gehen wir!
